title: Choosing State Management in Flutter in 2026
excerpt: A practical walkthrough of Provider, Riverpod, and Bloc — when each shines and how to keep your codebase maintainable as the app grows.
content: State management is one of the first architectural decisions you make in a Flutter app — and one of the easiest to get wrong if you copy patterns without understanding the trade-offs.

Provider remains a solid default for smaller teams: it is approachable, well documented, and plays nicely with the framework. When complexity grows, Riverpod adds compile-time safety and better test ergonomics. Bloc shines when you want explicit, event-driven flows and predictable state machines.

Whichever you pick, keep boundaries clear: UI listens to state, business logic lives outside widgets, and side effects stay in one place. That discipline matters more than the library name on the tin.

title: Profiling Flutter Apps Without the Guesswork
excerpt: How I use DevTools, frame timing, and rebuild tracking to find jank before users do — plus a short checklist for release builds.
content: Performance work starts in profile mode, not release guesses. Flutter DevTools gives you a timeline of frames, GPU work, and expensive rebuilds — use it early when something feels sluggish.

I watch for rebuild storms: a single ChangeNotifier fanning out too wide, or lists rebuilding entire subtrees. Sometimes the fix is a const constructor; sometimes it is restructuring state so only the leaf that needs to paint actually invalidates.

Before shipping, run through a short checklist: profile on a mid-range device, scroll your heaviest screens for thirty seconds, and confirm you are not blocking the UI isolate on I/O or large JSON parses.

title: Design Systems That Actually Work for Mobile Teams
excerpt: Tokens, components, and documentation patterns that help designers and Flutter devs stay aligned from MVP to production.
content: A design system on mobile is not just a Figma file — it is the contract between design and engineering. Tokens for color, type, and spacing should map cleanly to ThemeData and reusable widgets.

Name components the way your team talks about them: PrimaryButton, not BlueRoundedThing. Document variants (loading, disabled, destructive) next to the widget API so nobody has to guess from screenshots.
Start small: ship a handful of high-traffic components perfectly, then grow. A thin system used consistently beats a thick system that nobody adopts.
